title: Adjusting with the seasons
hook: a rule bends for Advent, Lent, illness, busy years
tomorrow: why would a prophet write so a runner could read it?

segments.voice: Last week ended with company for the road: Mary, and a saint for the year. A new week, and a rule meets real life.
screen: `COMPANY FOR THE ROAD.` → `A RULE MEETS REAL LIFE.`

segments.voice: What happens to a rule when life breaks your routine? Start at noon, in a monastery, in summer. The brothers come in from the fields, sunburned, and eat together. Then the bell doesn't call them back to work. The Rule of Saint Benedict tells them to lie down on their beds, in silence. Anyone who'd rather read may read quietly to himself. A nap, written into a rule for monks. But isn't a rule supposed to be the same every day?
screen: `NOON, IN SUMMER.` → `LIE DOWN ON YOUR BEDS.` → `ISN'T A RULE THE SAME EVERY DAY?`

segments.voice: Not Benedict's. His Rule sets one schedule for summer and another for winter, because the light and the work change. In Lent it asks each monk to add something of his own: some extra prayer, some going without. For the sick it bends the furthest: care for them comes before everything, with food and rest the others don't get. The old and the young get allowances too. The core stays: the prayer, the community, the work. The shape moves with the season. Ecclesiastes says it in the Douay-Rheims: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." One to tell a friend: the Catechism says a serious reason, like illness or the care of an infant, excuses a Catholic from Sunday Mass. Even the center of the week bends for a sick child. So a personal rule bends too: fuller in Advent and Lent, quieter in a brutal semester, very small in the year of a newborn or a diagnosis. Bending isn't quitting. A rule that can't bend can snap in the first busy month, and then it's gone. A rule that bends is still there when the season turns.
screen: `A NAP, WRITTEN INTO THE RULE.` · `LENT ADDS; SICKNESS EASES.` · `ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR SEASON.` · `THE CORE STAYS.` · then, large: `IT BENDS, NOT BREAKS.`

segments.voice: Try wish, obstacle, plan. Wish: one practice from your rule you most want to keep. Obstacle: the season most likely to break it, like finals, a new job, a long illness. Plan: the smaller version you'll do then, one decade instead of a rosary, one verse instead of a chapter.
Adjusting with the seasons. A rule that grows in Lent, shrinks in sickness, and keeps its core all year.
Hold onto this: it bends, not breaks, like a monastery that naps in summer. Day 1744, done.

howItsDone: Catholics often adjust their prayer and practices with the liturgical seasons, adding a sacrifice or extra prayer in Advent and Lent, and simplifying in illness, after a birth or in demanding stretches of life.

chat.says: rolled my ankle. no running for two weeks. my rule starts with a 6am run and a rosary. now what?
options: Bend it: keep 6 a.m. and the rosary, and ice where the run was.
Pause the whole rule till you heal, then restart it fresh.
Run anyway. A rule that bends for pain isn't really a rule.
chat.meaning: Benedict's Rule eases for the sick and keeps its core. A rule that bends with the season is still there when the season turns.

Saint Benedict.meaning: an Italian monk whose Rule shaped Western monastic life

Lent.meaning: the season of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter

Advent.meaning: the season of waiting and preparing before Christmas

Ecclesiastes.meaning: an Old Testament book of wisdom about time and life

Catechism.meaning: the Church's official summary of Catholic teaching
